title: Concurrency & Parallelism
summary: Concurrency is dealing with many things at once; parallelism is doing many at once. The moment two flows touch the same data, you inherit the hardest bugs of your career.

blocks.markdown:
Concurrency is about **structure**; parallelism is about **execution**.

- **Concurrency** — dealing with many tasks at once by interleaving them, even on one core.
- **Parallelism** — literally running tasks at the same instant, which needs multiple cores.
- One chef juggling three dishes is concurrency; three chefs cooking at once is parallelism.
- The danger starts the moment two flows touch the **same shared data**.

blocks.subTitle: Pick the right tool
blocks.markdown:
Match the model to the workload.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| I/O-bound, many connections | Async / event loop |
| CPU-bound, spare cores | Threads / processes |
| Shared counter on hot path | Atomic / CAS |
| Multi-step invariant | Mutex |
| Many stateful entities | Actor model |

blocks.subTitle: Threads share memory
blocks.markdown:
A thread is a path of execution inside a process; threads in one process **share the heap**.

- A **process** has private memory; a **thread** lives inside it and shares globals and objects.
- Each thread keeps its own **stack** (locals, call frames) but shares everything on the heap.
- Sharing is the power — passing data is just a pointer, no copying.
- Sharing is also the danger — two threads writing the same memory with no coordination corrupts it.

blocks.subTitle: Race conditions
blocks.markdown:
A race condition is a bug where correctness depends on the **timing** of interleaving.

![Two threads interleaving a read-modify-write and losing an update](assets/c02-concurrency-parallelism/race-condition.svg)

- `count = count + 1` is really three steps: **read**, **add**, **write back**.
- Two threads can both read `0`, both write `1` — one increment silently lost.
- The bug only fires on the unlucky interleaving, so tests pass and production corrupts.
- The fix: make the dangerous **critical section** atomic — at most one thread inside at a time.

assets.alt: Two threads interleaving a read-modify-write and losing an update

blocks.subTitle: Mutexes
blocks.markdown:
A mutex enforces mutual exclusion: lock before the critical section, unlock after.

```text
mutex m
function increment():
    m.lock()
    count = count + 1     # only one thread here at a time
    m.unlock()
```

- Only the holder may unlock; others trying to lock **wait**.
- Correct and easy to reason about, but a contended lock **serializes** work you hoped ran in parallel.
- Hold locks for as short a time as possible.

blocks.subTitle: Deadlock's four conditions
blocks.markdown:
Deadlock needs **all four** Coffman conditions at once — break any one to prevent it.

![Two threads forming a wait-for cycle over two locks](assets/c02-concurrency-parallelism/deadlock-cycle.svg)

- **Mutual exclusion** — a resource is held by only one thread.
- **Hold and wait** — hold one resource while waiting for another.
- **No preemption** — only the holder releases a resource.
- **Circular wait** — a cycle of threads each waiting on the next.

The common fix breaks circular wait: always acquire locks in a **fixed global order**.

assets.alt: Two threads forming a wait-for cycle over two locks

blocks.subTitle: Atomics & compare-and-swap
blocks.markdown:
For a single variable, a lock is overkill — use an atomic CAS retry loop.

```text
repeat:
    old = counter.load()
    new = old + 1
until counter.CAS(expected=old, new=new)
```

- **CAS** sets memory to `new` only if it still holds `expected`, in one atomic step.
- Far cheaper than a mutex on the uncontended path; the basis of **lock-free** code.
- Under heavy contention the retry loop can **spin** and waste cycles.
- **ABA problem**: a value goes A to B back to A, so CAS wrongly thinks nothing changed; fix with version tags.

blocks.subTitle: The memory model
blocks.markdown:
Threads can see **stale** or **reordered** values — neither visibility nor order is free.

- **Visibility** — a write may sit in a core's store buffer, so another core reads a stale value.
- **Reordering** — compiler and CPU reorder freely as long as a single thread's result looks right.
- A **memory barrier** forbids reordering and flushes writes; you get them via locks, atomics, or `volatile`.
- These establish **happens-before**: A's work before releasing a lock is visible to B after acquiring it.
- Sharing plain variables with no such edge is a **data race** — undefined behavior.

blocks.subTitle: Event loop & actors
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to get concurrency without lock bugs.

![Producers and consumers exchanging items through a fixed-size buffer](assets/c02-concurrency-parallelism/producer-consumer.svg)

- **Event loop** — one thread never blocks; on I/O it registers a callback and runs other ready work. Huge concurrency for **I/O-bound** load, but a CPU-heavy callback stalls everything.
- **Actor model** — actors own private state and a mailbox, talking only by **immutable messages**. No shared memory means no data races by construction.
- **Producer-consumer** decouples makers from doers via a bounded buffer (shown above) with back-pressure.

assets.alt: Producers and consumers exchanging items through a fixed-size buffer

blocks.subTitle: Threads vs async
blocks.markdown:
Both give concurrency — they trade differently.

| Aspect | Threads | Async loop |
|---|---|---|
| Parallelism | Multi-core | One core |
| Cost per wait | ~1 MB stack | Cheap |
| Model | Blocking | Non-blocking |
| Best for | CPU-bound | I/O-bound |

Threads use cores but cost memory and context switches; async holds many idle waits cheaply but can't span cores alone.

blocks.subTitle: Picking a primitive
blocks.markdown:
Start coarse and correct; refine only where a profiler proves contention.

- **Single variable, hot path** → atomic / CAS, no lock overhead.
- **Multi-step invariant** → mutex; clarity beats cleverness.
- **Cap concurrency** (connection pool) → counting **semaphore**, an ownerless counter to N.
- **Wait for a condition** → condition variable, never a busy-spin loop.
- **Many stateful entities** → actor model to kill data races by design.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & signals
blocks.markdown:
These models run the systems you use daily.

- **Java `ConcurrentHashMap`** — pushed locking from whole-map down to one bucket, using CAS on the fast path ([a03-hashing](a03-hashing.md)).
- **Redis** — one thread with an event loop makes each command atomic, no locks ([b05-caching](b05-caching.md)).
- **Nginx / Node.js** — event loops over `epoll` serve huge connection counts; Nginx adds a worker per core.
- **Erlang / WhatsApp** — millions of lightweight actors per server for fault isolation.
- **Watch** rising thread-pool queue depth, lock wait time, and **event-loop lag** in production.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Concurrency means faster."** It adds coordination cost; with one core and CPU-bound work it can be slower.
- **"`volatile` makes it atomic."** It guarantees visibility only — `volatile count++` still races.
- **"More threads = more throughput."** Past the core count you pay context-switch and contention costs.
- **"Tests pass, so no race."** Races surface once in millions of runs; use race detectors.
- **`if` instead of `while`** on a condition variable — spurious and stolen wakeups break it.
